units.la: Sathan is now in his passions, hee feeles his passion approaching ; he loves to fish in royled waters. Though that Dragon cannot sting the vitals of the Elect mortally,yet that Beelzebub can fly-blow their Intellectuals miserably: The finer Religion grows, the finer he spins his Cobwebs, he will hold pace with Christ so long as his wits will serve him. Hee sees himselfe beaten out of grosse Idolatries, Heresies, Ceremonies, where the Light breakes forth with power ; he will therefore bestirre him to prevaricate Evangelicall Truths, and Ordinances, that if they will needs be walking, yet they shall laborare varicibus, and not keep their path : he will put them out of time and place ; Assascinating for his Engineers,men of Paracelsian parts, well compl xioned [?] for honesty ; for, such are fittest to Mountebanke his Chimistry into sicke Churches and weake Judgements.
units.tr: Satan is now in his element; he feels his passion coming on and loves to fish in troubled waters. Though that dragon cannot sting the vitals of the Elect to death, yet that Beelzebub can fly-blow their intellects grievously. The finer Religion grows, the finer he spins his cobwebs. He will keep pace with Christ for as long as his wits serve him. He sees himself beaten out of gross idolatries, heresies and ceremonies wherever the light breaks forth with power, so he will bestir himself to pervert the evangelical truths and ordinances, so that, if they must still walk, they shall limp on crooked legs and not keep their course. He will put them out of their time and place, using as his assassins for his engineers men of Paracelsian gifts, well complexioned for honesty; for such are the fittest to peddle his chemistry, like mountebanks, among sick Churches and weak judgements.

units.la: Nor shall hee neede to stretch his strength overmuch in this worke: Too many men having not laid their foundation sure, nor ballasted their Spirits deep with humility and feare, are prest enough of themselves to evaporate their owne apprehensions. Those that are acquainted with Story know, it hath ever been so in new Editions of Churches: Such as are least able, are most busy to pudder in the rubbish, and to raise dust in the eyes of more steady Repayrers. Civill Commotions make room for uncivill practises: Religious mutations, for irreligious opinions: Change of aire, discovers corrupt bodies: Reformation of Religion, unsound mindes. He that hath any well-faced phancy in his Crowne, and doth not vent it now, feares, the pride of his own heart will dub him duns for ever. Such a one will trouble the whole Israel of God with his most untimely births, though he makes the bones of his vanity stick up, to the view and griefe of all that are godly wise. The devill desires no better sport then to see light heads handle their heeles, and fetch their carreers in a time, when the Roofe of Liberty stands open.
units.tr: Nor will he need to exert himself much in this work. Many men, who have not laid their foundations firmly or weighted their spirits deeply with humility and fear, are quick enough, of their own accord, to let their own notions evaporate. Those who know history know it has always been so when churches are reissued in new editions. Those least able are most eager to stir about in the rubbish and throw dust in the eyes of the steadier repairers. Civil commotions make room for uncivil practices, and religious upheavals for irreligious opinions. A change of air reveals corrupt bodies; the reformation of religion reveals unsound minds. Whoever has some showy fancy in his head and does not air it now fears that the pride of his own heart will make a dunce of him forever. Such a man will trouble the whole Israel of God with his most untimely offspring, though he thrusts up the bones of his vanity for all the godly wise to see, to their grief. The devil desires no better sport than to see light heads caper and run their courses when the roof of liberty stands open.

units.la: The next perplexed Queftion, with pious and ponderous men, will be : What should be done for the healing of these comfortlesse exulcerations? I am the unableft adviser of a thousand, the unworthiest of ten thousand ; yet I hope I may presume to assert what follows without just offence.
units.tr: The next perplexing question, with pious and weighty men, will be: what should be done for the healing of these comfortless ulcerations? I am the most unable adviser of a thousand, the unworthiest of ten thousand; yet I hope I may presume to assert what follows without just offence.

units.la: If the devill might have his free option, I beleeve he would ask nothing else, but liberty to enfranchize all other Religions, and to embondage the true; nor should he need: It is much to be feared, that laxe Tolerations upon State-pretences and planting necessities, will be the next subtle Stratagem he will spread, to distate the Truth of God and supplant the peace of the Churches. Tolerations in things tolerable, exquisitely drawn out by the lines of the Scripture, and penfill of the Spirit, are the sacred favours of Truth, the due latitudes of Love, the faire Compartiments of Christian fraternity: but irregular dispensations, dealt forth by the facilities of men, are the frontiers of error, the redoubts of Schisme, the perillous irritaments of carnall enmity.
units.tr: If the devil might have his free option, I believe he would ask nothing else but liberty to enfranchise all other religions and to embondage the true; nor would he need to: it is much to be feared that lax tolerations, upon state pretences and planting necessities, will be the next subtle stratagem he will spread, to distaste the truth of God and supplant the peace of the churches. Tolerations in things tolerable, exquisitely drawn out by the lines of Scripture and the pencil of the Spirit, are the sacred favours of truth, the due latitudes of love, the fair compartments of Christian fraternity; but irregular dispensations, dealt forth by the facilities of men, are the frontiers of error, the redoubts of schism, the perilous irritants of carnal enmity.

units.la: My heart hath naturally detested foure things: The standing of the Apocrypha in the Bible; Forreiners dwelling in my Countrey, to crowd out native Subjects into the corners of the Earth; Alchymized coines; Tolerations of divers Religions, or of one Religion in segregant shapes: He that willingly assents to the last, if he examines his heart by day-light, his conscience will tell him, he is either an Atheist, or an Heretique, or an Hypocrite, or at best a captive to some lust: polchpiety is the greatest impiety in the world. True Religion is Ignis probationis, which doth congregare homogenea & segregare heterogenia.
units.tr: My heart has always detested four things: the standing of the Apocrypha in the Bible; foreigners living in my country, so that they crowd native subjects into the corners of the earth; alchemized coins; and tolerations of divers religions, or of one religion in segregated shapes. Anyone who willingly assents to the last, if he examines his heart by daylight, will find that his conscience tells him he is either an atheist, a heretic, a hypocrite, or at best a captive to some lust. Half-piety is the greatest impiety in the world. True religion is the fire of testing, which gathers together the homogeneous and separates the heterogeneous.

units.la: I would willingly hope that no Member of the Parliament hath skilfully ingratiated himselfe into the hearts of the House, that he might watch a time to midwife out some ungracious Toleration for his own turne, and for the sake of that, some others. I would also hope that a word of generall caution should not bee particularly misapplied. Yet good Gentlemen, looke well about you, and remember how Tiberius plaid the Fox with the Senate of Rome, and how Fabius Maximus cropt his eares for his cunning.
units.tr: I would willingly hope that no member of Parliament has skilfully ingratiated himself into the hearts of the House so that he might watch for a time to midwife out some ungracious toleration for his own turn, and for the sake of that, some others. I would also hope that a word of general caution should not be particularly misapplied. Yet, good gentlemen, look well about you, and remember how Tiberius played the fox with the Senate of Rome, and how Fabius Maximus cropped his ears for his cunning.

units.la: That State is wise, that will improve all paines and patience rather to compose, then tolerate differences in Religion. There is no divine Truth, but hath much Celestiall fire in it from the Spirit of Truth: nor no irreligious untruth, without its proportion of Antifire from the Spirit of Error to contradict it: the zeale of the one, the virulency of the other, must necessarily kindle Combustions. Fiery diseases seated in the spirit, embroile the whole frame of the body; others more externall and coole, are lesse dangerous. They which divide in Religion, divide in God ; they who divide in him, divide beyond Genus Generalissimum, where there is no reconciliation, without atonement; that is, without uniting in him, who is One, and in his Truth, which is also one.
units.tr: That state is wise which will spend all its pains and patience to compose differences in religion rather than tolerate them. There is no divine truth that does not have much celestial fire in it from the Spirit of Truth, nor any irreligious untruth without its proportion of counter-fire from the spirit of error to contradict it. The zeal of the one and the virulence of the other must necessarily kindle combustions. Fiery diseases seated in the spirit throw the whole frame of the body into confusion; others that are more external and cool are less dangerous. Those who divide in religion divide in God; and those who divide in Him divide beyond the highest genus, where there is no reconciliation without atonement, that is, without uniting in Him who is One, and in His Truth, which is also one.

units.la: Concerning Tolerations I may further assert.
units.tr: Concerning tolerations I may further assert:

units.la: That Perfecution of true Religion, and Toleration of false are the Fannes and Fambres to the Kingdome of Christ, whereof the last is farre the worst. Augustines tongue had not owed his mouth one penny-rent though it had never spake word more in it, but this, Nullum malum pejus libertate errandi.
units.tr: That persecution of true religion and toleration of false religion are the Jannes and Jambres of the kingdom of Christ, of which the last is by far the worse. Augustine's tongue would not have owed his mouth a penny of rent, even if it had never spoken another word, than this: No evil is worse than the liberty to err.

units.la: He that is willing to tolerate any unsound Opinion, that his owne may also be tolerated, though never so found, will for a need hang Gods Bible at the Devills girdle.
units.tr: Whoever is willing to tolerate any unsound opinion, so that his own may also be tolerated, however sound it is, will for need hang God's Bible at the devil's girdle.

units.la: Every Toleration of false Religions, or Opinions hath as many Errors and sinnes in it, as all the false Religions and Opinions it tolerates, and one found one more.
units.tr: Every toleration of false religions or opinions has as many errors and sins in it as all the false religions and opinions it tolerates, and one more besides.

units.la: That State that will give Liberty of Conscience in matters of Religion, must give Liberty of Conscience and Conversation in their Morall Lawes, or else the Fiddle will be out of tune, and some of the strings cracke.
units.tr: That state which gives liberty of conscience in matters of religion must give liberty of conscience and conduct in its moral laws as well, or else the fiddle will be out of tune and some of the strings will crack.

units.la: He that will rather make an irreligious quarrell with other Religions, then try the Truth of his own by valuable Arguments, and peaceable Sufferings; either his Religion, or himselfe is irreligious.
units.tr: Whoever would rather pick an irreligious quarrel with other religions than test the truth of his own by valid arguments and peaceable sufferings is either irreligious in his religion or irreligious in himself.

units.la: Experience will teach Churches and Christians, that it is farre better to live in a State united, though somewhat Corrupt, then in a State, whereof some Partis Incorrupt, and all the rest divided.
units.tr: Experience will teach Churches and Christians that it is far better to live in a state united, though somewhat corrupt, than in a state where some part is incorrupt and all the rest divided.

units.la: I am not altogether ignorant of the eight Rules given by Orthodox Divines, about giving Tolerations, yet with their favour I dare affirme,
units.tr: I am not altogether ignorant of the eight rules given by orthodox divines about granting toleration, yet with their favour I dare affirm,

units.la: That there is no Rule given by God for any State to give an Affirmative Toleration to any false Religion, or Opinion whatsoever ; they must connive in some Cases, but may not concede in any.
units.tr: That there is no rule given by God for any state to grant an affirmative toleration to any false religion or opinion whatsoever. They may connive in some cases, but they may not concede in any.

units.la: That the State of England (so farre as my Intelligence serves) might in time have prevented with ease, and may yet without any great difficulty deny both Toleration, and Connivances salva Republica.
units.tr: That the State of England (so far as my intelligence serves) might in time have prevented this with ease, and may yet, without any great difficulty, deny both toleration and connivance with the commonwealth safe.

units.la: That if the State of England shall either willingly Tolerate, or weakly connive at such Courses, the Church of that Kingdome will sooner become the Devills Dancing-Schoole, then Gods-Temple: The Civill State a Beare-garden, then an Exchange: The whole Realme a Pais base, then an England. And what pity it is, that that Country which hath been the Staple of Truth to all Christendome, should now become the Aviary of Errors to the whole World, let every fearing heart judge.
units.tr: That if the State of England shall either willingly tolerate, or weakly connive at such courses, the Church of that kingdom will sooner become the Devil's dancing-school than God's temple; the civil state a bear-garden rather than an exchange; the whole realm a base country rather than an England. And what a pity it is that that country which has been the staple of truth to all Christendom should now become the aviary of errors to the whole world, let every fearing heart judge.

units.la: I take Liberty of Conscience to bee nothing but a freedome from sinne, and error. Conscientia in tantum libera, in quantum ab errore liberata. And liberty of Error nothing but a Prison for Conscience. Then small will bee the kindnesse of a State to build such Prisons for their Subjects.
units.tr: I take liberty of conscience to be nothing but freedom from sin and error. A conscience is free only so far as it has been freed from error. And liberty of error is nothing but a prison for conscience. Then small will be the kindness of a state that builds such prisons for its subjects.

units.la: If two Centers (as we may suppose) be in one Circle, and lines drawn from both to all the points of the Compasse, they will certainly crosse one another, and probably cut through the Centers themselves.
units.tr: If two centres (as we may suppose) lie in one circle, and lines are drawn from both to all the points of the compass, they will certainly cross one another, and probably cut through the centres themselves.

units.la: There is talke of an universall Toleration, I would talk what I could against it, did I know what more apt and reasonable Sacrifice England could offer to God for his late performing all his heavenly Truths, then an universall Toleration of all hellish Errors, or how they shall make an universall Reformation, but by making Christs Academy the Devils Vniversity, where any man may commence Heretique per saltum; where he that is filius Diabolicus, or simpliciter pessimus, may have his grace to goe to hell cum Publico Privilegio; and carry as many after him, as he can.
units.tr: There is talk of a universal toleration. I would speak what I could against it, did I know what more fitting and reasonable sacrifice England could offer to God for his late performance of all his heavenly truths than a universal toleration of all hellish errors. Or how will they make a universal reformation, except by making Christ's academy the devil's university, where any man may become a heretic at a bound, where he who is a son of the devil, or simply the worst, may have his licence to go to hell with public privilege, and carry as many after him as he can.

units.la: Religio docenda est, non coercenda is a pretty piece of album Latinum for some kinde of throats that are willingly sore, but Haresis dedocenda est non permittenda, will be found in a farre better Diamoron for the Gargarismes garisfmes this Age wants, if timely, and throughly applyed.
units.tr: Religion is to be taught, not coerced is a pretty piece of Latin for the schoolroom for some kind of throats that are willingly sore. But heresy is to be unlearned, not permitted will be found in a far better electuary, the Diamoron, for the gargles this age lacks, if it is applied in good time and thoroughly.

units.la: If there be roome in England for Familifts ... Manes Libertines ... Lemures Erastians ... Dryades Antitrinitarians ... Homadryades Anabaptifts, ... Potamides Antiscripturifts ... Naiades Arminians ... Hinnides Manifestarians ... Pierides Millinaries ... Nereides Antinomians ... Pales Socinians ... Anpnides Arrians ... Parcades Perfectifts ... Castalides Brownifts ... Monides Mortalians ... Charites Religious Men Seekers ... Heliconides but pernicious Enthusiasts, ... Pegasides. Heretiques. &c. ... &c. then room for Good Spirits, but very Devills.
units.tr: If there be room in England for Familists ... Shades, Libertines ... Ghosts, Erastians ... Wood-nymphs, Antitrinitarians ... Tree-nymphs, Anabaptists ... River-nymphs, Antiscripturists ... Water-nymphs, Arminians ... Mules, Manifestarians ... Muses, Millenaries ... Sea-nymphs, Antinomians ... Goddesses of shepherds, Socinians ... Wind-nymphs, Arians ... Fates, Perfectists ... Castalian nymphs, Brownists ... Solitaries, Mortalists ... Graces, religious men, Seekers ... Muses of Helicon, but pernicious enthusiasts ... Pegasides, heretics, &c. ... &c., then there is room for good spirits, but very devils.

units.la: In a word room for Hell above ground.
units.tr: In a word, room for Hell above ground.

units.la: Fourthly, to make speedy provifion against Obstinates and disseminaries : where under favour, two things will be found requisite. First, variety of penaltyes, I meane certaine, not indefinite : I am a Crabbat against Arbitrary Government. Experience ence hath taught us here, that politicall, domesticall, and personall respects, will not admit one and the same remedy for all, without sad inconveniences. Secondly, Just severity: persecution hath ever spread Truth, prosecution scatterd Errour: Ten of the most Christian Emperors, found that way best; Schollars know whom I meane: Five of the ancient fathers perswaded to it, of whom Augustine was one, who for a time argued hard for Indulgency: but upon conference with other prudent Bishops, altered his judgement, as appears in three of his Epistles, to Marcellinus, Donatus, and Boniface. I would be understood, not onely an Allower, but an humble Petitioner, that ignorant and tender conscienced Anabaptists may have due time and means of conviction.
units.tr: Fourthly, to make speedy provision against obstinate persons and disseminators of error, I think two things will be found necessary, with your permission. First, a variety of penalties, by which I mean fixed ones, not indefinite ones. I am a cross-grained opponent of arbitrary government. Experience has taught us here that political, domestic and personal circumstances will not allow one and the same remedy for everyone without grievous inconvenience. Secondly, just severity. Persecution has always spread the truth; prosecution has scattered error. Ten of the most Christian emperors found this way best; scholars know whom I mean. Five of the ancient Fathers urged it, of whom Augustine was one, who for a time argued strongly for leniency, but after conference with other prudent bishops changed his judgement, as appears in three of his letters, to Marcellinus, Donatus and Boniface. I would be understood not merely as one who allows this, but as a humble petitioner that ignorant and tender-conscienced Anabaptists may be given due time and means of conviction.

units.la: Brethren, have an extraordinary care also of the late Theosophers, that teach men to climbe to heaven upon a ladder of lying figments. Rather then the devill will lose his game, he will out-shoot Christ in his own bow ; he will outlaw the Law, quite out of the word and world: over-Gospell the Gospell, and quidanye Christ, with Sugar and Rats-bane. He was Professour not long since at Schelstat in Alsatia, where be learned, that no poyson is so deadly as the poyson of Grace.
units.tr: Brethren, have an extraordinary care also of the late Theosophers, who teach men to climb to heaven upon a ladder of lying fictions. Rather than the devil lose his game, he will outshoot Christ with his own bow; he will outlaw the Law quite out of the word and the world; he will over-Gospel the Gospel, and what-d'ye-call-him Christ, with sugar and rat's-bane. He was a professor not long since at Schelstat in Alsatia, where he learned that no poison is so deadly as the poison of grace.

units.la: I cannot imagine why the Holy Ghoft should give Tim: the solemneft charge, was ever given mortall man, to observe the Rules he had given, till the coming of Christ, if new things must be expected.
units.tr: I cannot imagine why the Holy Ghost should give Timothy the solemnest charge ever given to a mortal man, to observe the rules he had given until the coming of Christ, if new things must be expected.

units.la: Woe be to them, who ever they be, that so trouble the wayes of God that they who have found the way to heaven, cannot finde the way to Church : And woe be to them, that so gaze at the glorious light, they say, will breake forth in the thousand yeares to come, that they make little of the gracious Truth that hath been revealed these sixteen hundred years past. And woe be to them that so under-value the first Master-Builders, I mean the Apostles of Christ, that unlesse he sends wiser then they, He must be accounted lesse faithfull in his house than Moses was.
units.tr: Woe be to them, whoever they be, who so trouble the ways of God that those who have found the way to heaven cannot find the way to church. And woe be to them who so gaze at the glorious light they say will break forth in the thousand years to come that they make little of the gracious truth that has been revealed these sixteen hundred years past. And woe be to them who so undervalue the first master-builders, I mean the apostles of Christ, that unless he sends wiser men than they, he must be accounted less faithful in his house than Moses was.

units.la: I have cause enough to be as charitable to others as any man living; yet I cannot but fear, that those men never Moored their Anchors well in the firme soile of Heaven, that are weather-wast up and down with every eddy-wind of every new Doctrine. The good Spirit of God doth not usually tie up the Helme, and suffer passengers to Heaven to ride a drift, hither and thither, as every wave and current carryes them: that is a fitter course for such as the Apostle calls wandring Starres and Meteors, without any certain motion, hurryed about with tempests, bred of the Exhalations of their own pride and self-wittednesse: whose damnation sleepeth not, and to whom the mist of darknesse is reserved for ever, that they may suffer irreparable shipwrack upon the Sands and Rocks of their own Errours, being of old ordained to condemnation.
units.tr: I have cause enough to be as charitable to others as any man living; yet I cannot but fear that those men never moored their anchors well in the firm soil of heaven who are weather-wasted up and down by every eddy-wind of every new doctrine. The good Spirit of God does not usually tie up the helm and suffer passengers to heaven to ride adrift, hither and thither, as every wave and current carries them. That is a fitter course for such as the Apostle calls wandering stars and meteors, without any certain motion, hurried about with tempests bred of the exhalations of their own pride and self-wittedness: whose damnation sleeps not, and to whom the mist of darkness is reserved for ever, so that they may suffer irreparable shipwreck upon the sands and rocks of their own errors, being of old ordained to condemnation.

units.la: Hence it is, that God is so jealous of his Truths, that he hath taken order in his due Justice : First, that no practicall sin is so sinfull as some errour in judgement; no men so accursed with indelible infamy and dedolent impenitency, as Authours of Heresie. Secondly, that the least Error, if grown sturdy and pressed, shall set open the Spittle doore of all the squint-ey'd, wry-necked, and brasen-faced Errors that are or ever were of that litter ; if they be not enough to serve its turne, it will beget more, though it hath not one cruft of reason to maintain them. Thirdly, that that State which will permit Errors in Religion, shall admit Errors in Policy unavoydably. Fourthly, that that Policy which will suffer irreligious errors, shall suffer the losse of so much Liberty in one kinde or other, I will not exempt Venice, Rhaguse, the Nether-lands, or any.
units.tr: Hence it is that God is so jealous of his Truths that he has taken order, in his due Justice: First, that no practical sin is so sinful as some error in judgement; no men so accursed with indelible infamy and dead impenitency as the authors of heresy. Secondly, that the least error, if it grows sturdy and is pressed, will set open the spittle door of all the squint-eyed, wry-necked and brazen-faced errors that are or ever were of that litter; if they are not enough to serve its turn, it will beget more, though it has not one crumb of reason to maintain them. Thirdly, that the state which will permit errors in religion shall unavoidably admit errors in policy. Fourthly, that the policy which will suffer irreligious errors shall suffer the loss of so much liberty in one kind or another; I will not exempt Venice, Ragusa, the Netherlands, or any.

units.la: Ye fay, why come not we over to help the Lord againft the Mighty, in thefe his Sacred battailes ?
units.tr: Ye say, why come not we over to help the Lord against the mighty in these his sacred battles?

units.la: In the mean time, we defire to bow our knees before the Throne of Grace day and night, that the Lord would be pleafed in his tender mercy to ftill the fad unquietneffe and per-peracute contentions, of that moft comfortable and renowned iland, that at length He may have praise in his Churches, and his Churches peace in him, through Jesus Christ.
units.tr: In the meantime, we desire to bow our knees before the throne of grace day and night, that the Lord would be pleased, in his tender mercy, to still the sad unquietness and perpetual contentions of that most comfortable and renowned island, that at length He may have praise in his Churches, and his Churches peace in Him, through Jesus Christ.

units.la: Ridentem dicere verum, quid prohibet?
units.tr: What prevents one from telling the truth with a smile?

units.la: Gray Gravity it selfe can well beteame,That Language be adapted to the Theme. He that to Parrots speaks, must parrotise; He that instructs a foole, may act th'unwise.
units.tr: Grey gravity itself may well allow that the language be fitted to the theme. He who speaks to parrots must parrot; he who instructs a fool may act the fool.

units.la: The very troublers and impoverishers of mankind. I can hardly forbeare to commend to the world a saying of a Lady living sometime with the Queen of Bohemiah, I know not where she found it, but it is pitty it should be lost. The world is full of care, much like unto a bubble; Women and care, and care and women, and women and (care and trouble.
units.tr: They are the very troublers and impoverishers of mankind. I can hardly forbear to commend to the world a saying of a lady who once lived with the Queen of Bohemia. I do not know where she found it, but it is a pity it should be lost: The world is full of care, much like unto a bubble; women and care, and care and women, and women and care and trouble.

units.la: But now our Roses are turned to Flore de lices, our Carnations to Tulips, our Gilliflowers to pansies, our City-Dames, to an indenominable Quæmalry of overturcas'd things. Hee that makes Coates for the Moone, had need take measure every noone; and he that makes for women, every Moone, to keep them from Lunacy.
units.tr: But now our roses are turned to fleur-de-lis, our carnations to tulips, our gillyflowers to pansies, and our city dames to an indenominable quamalry of overturned things. He who makes coats for the moon had need take measure every noon, and he who makes for women must make every moon, to keep them from lunacy.

units.la: Most deare and unparallel'd Ladyes, be pleased to attempt it: as you have the precellency of the women of the world for beauty and feature; so assume the honour to give, and not take Law from any, in matter of attire: if ye can transact so faire a motion among your selves unanimously, I dare say, they that most renite, will least repent. What greater honour can your Honors desire, then to build a Promontory president to all foraigne Ladies, to deserve so eminently at the hands of all the English Gentry, present and to come: and to confute the opinion of all the wise men in the world; who never thought it possible for women to doe so good a work?
units.tr: Most dear and incomparable Ladies, be pleased to take this up. As you excel the women of the world in beauty and form, so take the honour of giving law, and not receiving it from anyone, in matters of dress. If you can carry so fair a motion through among yourselves unanimously, I dare say that those who most resist will least repent. What greater honour can your Honours desire than to build a conspicuous promontory of example for all foreign ladies, and to deserve so eminently at the hands of all the English gentry, present and to come, and to confute the opinion of all the wise men in the world, who never thought it possible for women to do so good a work?

units.la: I addresse my self to those who can both heare and mend all if they please: I seriously feare, if the pious Parliament doe not finde a time to state fashions, as ancient Parliaments have done in some part, God will hardly finde a time to state Religion or Peace: They are the surguedryes of pride, the wantonnesse of idlenesse, provoking sins, the certain prodromies of assured judgement, Zeph.1.7, 8.
units.tr: I address myself to those who can both hear and mend everything if they choose. I seriously fear that if the pious Parliament does not find time to regulate fashions, as ancient parliaments have in some measure done, God will hardly find time to settle religion or peace. These fashions are the arrogances of pride, the wantonness of idleness, sins that provoke God, and the certain forerunners of assured judgement, Zeph.1.7, 8.

units.la: When States dishelv'd are, and lawes untwist,
units.tr: When states are dishevelled, and laws unravelled,

units.la: Reformation.
units.tr: Reformation.

units.la: 1. When God shall purge this Land with soap and nitre, Woe be to the Crowne, woe be to the Mitre.
units.tr: 1. When God shall purge this land with soap and nitre, woe be to the Crown, woe be to the Mitre.

units.la: The accent of the blow shall fall there.
units.tr: The accent of the blow shall fall there.

units.la: He that pities not the Crowne, pities not his owne soule. Hee that pities not those that wore the Mitre, more than they pitied themselves, or the Churches over which they insulted, or the State then corrupted and now corrayned by their pride and negligence, isto blame.
units.tr: He who does not pity the Crown does not pity his own soul. He who does not pity those who wore the Mitre, more than they pitied themselves, or the churches over which they domineered, or the state then corrupted and now corroded by their pride and negligence, is to blame.

units.la: 2. There is a set of Bishops comming next behind, Will ride the divell off his legs, and break his wind.
units.tr: 2. There is a set of bishops coming next behind, who will ride the devil off his legs and break his wind.

units.la: J feare, if the Assembly of all Divines, do not consent, and concenter the sooner, God will breathe a spirit of wisdome and meeknesse, into the Parliament of no Divines, to whom the Imperative and Coactive power supremely belongs, to consult such a commoderate way, as shall best please him, and profit his Churches: so that it shall be written upon the doore of the Assembly; The Lord was not there.
units.tr: I fear that if the Assembly of all Divines does not consent, and concentre the sooner, God will breathe a spirit of wisdom and meekness into the Parliament of no Divines, to whom the imperative and coercive power supremely belongs, to consult such a moderate way as shall best please him and profit his Churches. So it shall be written upon the door of the Assembly: The Lord was not there.

units.la: J feare, he that sayes, the Presbyterian and Independent way, if rightly carryed, doe not meet in one, he doth not handle his Compasses so considerately as he should.
units.tr: I fear that he who says the Presbyterian and Independent way, if rightly carried, do not meet in one, does not handle his compasses so considerately as he should.

units.la: J feare, if Authority doth not establish a suteable and peaceable Government of Churches the sooner, the bells in all the steeples will ring awke so long, that they will hardly be brought into tune any more.
units.tr: I fear that if authority does not establish a suitable and peaceable government of Churches the sooner, the bells in all the steeples will ring awry so long that they will hardly be brought into tune any more.

units.la: J
units.tr: I

units.la: In matter of Reformation, this would be remembred, that in premonitory judgements, God will take good words, and sincere intents; but in peremptory, nothing but reall performances.
units.tr: In the matter of reformation, let this be remembered: in premonitory judgements God will accept good words and sincere intentions, but in peremptory judgements he will accept nothing but real performance.

units.la: Composition.
units.tr: Composition.

units.la: Si natura negat, facit indignatio versum They areQualemcunque potest ——Juvenal. these.
units.tr: If nature denies it, indignation makes the verse (Juvenal). Such as it can be (Juvenal). These are they.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: They seldome lose the field, but often win,That end their wars, before their wars begin.
units.tr: They seldom lose the field, but often win, who end their wars before their wars begin.

units.la: Their Cause is often worst, that first begin, And they may lose the field, the field that win:
units.tr: Their cause is often worst who first begin, and they may lose the field who win the field:

units.la: In Civill wars 'twixt Subjects and their King, There is no conquest got by conquering.
units.tr: In civil wars between subjects and their king, there is no conquest gained by conquering.

units.la: 4. War ill begun, the onely way to mend, Is to end the War before the war doe end.
units.tr: 4. A war ill begun has one way to mend: to end the war before the war does end.

units.la: 5. They that will end ill wars, must have the skill, To make an end by Rule, and not by Will.
units.tr: 5. They who will end ill wars must have the skill to make an end by rule, and not by will.

units.la: The crazie world will crack, in all the middle joynts, If all the ends it hath, have not their parapoynts.
units.tr: The crazy world will crack in all its middle joints, if all the ends it has do not have their pairings.

units.la: But I hope I may safely say, The body beares the head, the head the Crowne ; If both beare not alike, then one will downe.
units.tr: But I hope I may safely say: The body bears the head, the head the crown; if both bear not alike, then one will go down.

units.la: Distracted Nature, calls for distracting Remedies ; perturbing policies for disturbing cures : if one Extreame should not constitute its Anti-Extreame, all things would soon be in extremo: if ambitious windes get into Rulers Crownes, rebellious vapours will into Subjects Caps, be they stopt never so close: Yet the tongues of Times tell us of ten Preter-royall Usurpations, to one contra-civill Rebellion.
units.tr: A distracted nature calls for distracting remedies, and disturbing policies for disturbing cures. If one extreme did not produce its opposite extreme, all things would soon be at the extreme. If ambitious winds get into rulers' crowns, rebellious vapours will get into subjects' caps, however tightly they are stopped. Yet the tongues of the times tell us of ten usurpations beyond royal right for every one rebellion against civil authority.

units.la: He is a good King that undoeth not his Subjects, by any one of his unlimited Prerogatives : and they are a good People, that undoe not their Prince, by any one of their unbounded Liberties, be they the very leaft : J am fure either may, and J am lure neither would be trusted, how good soever. Stories tell us in effect, though not in termes, that over-rifen Kings, have been the next evills to the world, unto falne Angels ; and that over-franchized people, are devills with fmooth fnaffles in their mouthes. A King that lives by Law, lives by love ; and he that lives above Law, shall live under hatred doe what he can. Slavery and Knavery goe as seldome asunder, as Tyranny and Cruelty.
units.tr: He is a good king who does not undo his subjects by any one of his unlimited prerogatives, and they are a good people who do not undo their prince by any one of their unbounded liberties, however small those may be. I am sure either may do it, and I am sure neither would be trusted, however good they were. Stories tell us, in effect though not in so many words, that kings who have risen too high have been the next evils to the world after fallen angels, and that over-franchised peoples are devils with smooth snaffles in their mouths. A king who lives by law lives by love, and he who lives above law shall live under hatred, do what he can. Slavery and knavery go as seldom apart as tyranny and cruelty do.

units.la: Subjects their King, the King his Subjects greets, Whilome the Scepter and the Plough-staffe meets.
units.tr: Subjects greet their King, and the King his Subjects; once the Scepter and the Plough-staff met.

units.la: Pax quo carior, eo charior. A Peace well made, is likeliest then to hold, When 'tis both dearly bought and dearly sold.
units.tr: The dearer the peace, the dearer it is held. A peace well made will hold best when it is both dearly bought and dearly sold.

units.la: King Charles will joyne Himselfe to bitter Griefe, Then joyne to God, and prove a Godly Chiefe.
units.tr: King Charles will join himself to bitter grief, / Then join to God, and prove a godly chief.

units.la: I have obferved men to have two kindes of Wills, a Free-hold will, fuch as men hold in Capite of themfelves ; or a Copy-hold will, held at the will of other Lords or Ladies. I have read almoft all the Common Law of England, and fome Statutes ; yet I never read, that the Parliament held their will in fuch a Capite: their Tenure is Knight-fervice, and good Knight-fervice too, or elfe they are to blame. And I am fure, a King cannot hold by Copy, at the will of other Lords ; the Law calls that bafe tenure, inconfiftent with Royalty ; much more bafe is it, to hold at the will of Ladies. Apron-ftring tenure is very weak, tyed but of a flipping knot, which a childe may undoe, much more a King. It ftands not with our Queens honour to weare an Apron, much leffe her Husband, in the ftrings ; that were to infnare both him and her felf in many unfafeties. I never heard our King was Effeminate: to be a little Uxorious perfonally, is a vertuous vice in Oeconomicks ; but Royally, a vitious vertue in Politicks. To fpeak Englifh, Books and tongues tell us, the errour of thefe warres on our Kings part, proceeds from ill Counfellours. Ill Counfellours, are very ill Gamefters ; if they fee their own ftake a loofing, they will play away King, Queen, Bifhops, Knights, Rooks, Pawnes, and all, before they will turne up the board : they that play for lufts, will play away themfelves, and not leave themfelves fo much as a heart to repent ; and then there is no Market left, but Hell ; if the cafe be thus, it is to no end to look for any end, till one fide make an end of the other. They that at stake their Crownes and Honours set, Play lasting games, if Lust or Guilt doe bet.
units.tr: I have observed that men have two kinds of wills: a freehold will, such as men hold in capite of themselves, or a copyhold will, held at the pleasure of other lords or ladies. I have read almost all the common law of England, and some statutes, yet I never read that Parliament held its will in such a capite: its tenure is knight-service, and good knight-service too, or else they are to blame. And I am sure a King cannot hold by copy, at the will of other lords; the law calls that base tenure, inconsistent with royalty. Much more base is it to hold at the will of ladies. Apron-string tenure is very weak, tied with a slipping knot which a child may undo, much more a king. It does not befit our Queen's honour to wear an apron, much less for her husband to be in the strings; that would ensnare both him and herself in many insecurities. I never heard that our King was effeminate: to be a little uxorious in private life is a virtuous vice in household management, but in royal matters it is a vicious virtue in politics. To speak plainly, books and tongues tell us that the error of these wars on our King's part proceeds from ill counsellors. Ill counsellors are very bad gamesters: if they see their own stake going to loss, they will play away king, queen, bishops, knights, rooks, pawns, and all, before they will turn up the board. Those who play for lusts will play away themselves, and not leave themselves so much as a heart to repent; and then there is no market left but hell. If the case be thus, it is pointless to look for any end until one side makes an end of the other. They that at stake their crowns and honours set, play lasting games, if lust or guilt do bet.

units.la: Cessation.
units.tr: Cessation.

units.la: If God would vouchsafe to give his Majesties Religion and Reason, power to sling his wills head over the Wall, in matter of Composition, and his Subjests strength to throw their lusts after it; Armes would be soon laid down, and Peace soon taken up. They that are not at peace with God, are not at peace with themselves, whatever they think; and they that are not at peace with themselves, cannot be at peace with others, if occasion provokes, be their natures never so good.
units.tr: If God would grant his Majesty's religion and reason the power to fling his will over the wall, in matter of composition, and his subjects' strength to throw their lusts after it, arms would soon be laid down and peace soon taken up. Those who are not at peace with God are not at peace with themselves, whatever they think; and those who are not at peace with themselves cannot be at peace with others, if occasion provokes them, however good their natures.

units.la: -- gratia gratis data, gratisima.
units.tr: -- Grace freely given, most freely.

units.la: In Breaches integrant, 'tween Principalls of States, Due Justice may suppresse, but Love redintegrates.
units.tr: In breaches that integrate between the principals of states, due justice may suppress, but love restores.

units.la: I intreat him to confider that our King is not onely a man, but a King in affliction, Kings afflictions are beyond Subjects apprehensions; a Crown may happily ake as much as a whole Common-wealth.
units.tr: I entreat him to consider that our King is not only a man but a King in affliction. Kings' afflictions are beyond subjects' apprehension; a crown may perhaps ache as much as a whole commonwealth.

units.la: I desire him also to conceale himself as deeply as he can, if he cannot get a speciall pardon, to weare a Latitat, about his neck, or let him lie close under the Philosophers stone,and I'le warrant him for ever being found.
units.tr: I advise him also to hide himself as deeply as he can if he cannot obtain a special pardon: let him wear a latitat about his neck, or lie close under the philosopher's stone, and I will guarantee that he is never found.

units.la: If he be discovered, I counsell him to get his head set on faster than our New-England Taylors use to set on Buttons; Kings, and Kings Childrens memories are as keen as their Subjects wits.
units.tr: If he is discovered, I counsel him to get his head set on faster than our New England tailors are used to set on buttons; kings, and kings' children, have memories as keen as their subjects' wits.

units.la: Prosecution.
units.tr: Prosecution.

units.la: If Reformation, Composition, Cessation, can finde no admittance, there must and will be Prosecution: to which I would also speak briefely and indifferently still to both sides; and first to that, which I had rather call Royalists then Cavaliers; who if I mistake not, fight against the Truth.
units.tr: If Reformation, Composition and Cessation find no admittance, there must and will be Prosecution. To this I will also speak briefly and impartially to both sides. First, to those whom I would rather call Royalists than Cavaliers, who, if I am not mistaken, fight against the Truth.

units.la: Couragious Gentlemen, Yee that will stab him that gives you the lye ; take heed yee spend not your bloods, limbs and soules, in fighting for some untruth : and yee that will fling out the gantlet to him that calls you Coward, dishonour not your selves with such Cowardise, as to fight against Truth, meerly for feare of it. A thousand pities it is such gallant Spirits should spend their lives, honours, heritages and sweet relations in any warres, where, for ought many of them know, some false mistake commands in Chiefe.
units.tr: Honoured countrymen, be entreated to love Truth. If it does not love you in return, and does not repair all your losses, then install some untruth in its place as your general. If you will needs go to war, be persuaded to contend lawfully, wisely and steadfastly against all errors in Divinity and Policy. They are the cursed counter-mures, dropped portcullises, scouring angi-ports, sulphurous grenades, laden murderers, peevish caltrops and rascal desperadoes, which the Prince of Lies employs with all his skill and malice to maintain the walls and gates of his kingdom when Truth would enter in with grace and peace to save forlorn sinners and distressed commonwealths. Witness the present deplorable state of sundry States in Europe.

units.la: Honoured Country-men, bee intreated to love Truth : if it loves not you againe, and repaires not all your losses, then installl some untruth in its roome, for your Generall. If you will needs warre, be perswa-ded ded to contend lawfully, wisely and stedfastly against all Errors in Divinity and Policy: they are the cursed Counter-mures, dropt Portcullises, scowring Angi-ports, sulphurious Granado's, laden murtherers, peevish Galthropes, and rascall desparadoes, which the Prince of lyes imployes with all his skill and malice, to maintaine the walls and gates of his kingdome, when Truth would enter in, with grace and peace to save forlorne sinners, and distressed Commonwealths; witnesse the present deplorable estate of sundry States in Europe.
units.tr: Honoured countrymen, be entreated to love Truth. If it does not love you again and repair all your losses, then install some Untruth in its room as your general. If you will needs go to war, be persuaded to contend lawfully, wisely and steadfastly against all errors in Divinity and Policy. They are the cursed counter-mures, dropped portcullises, scouring angiports, sulphurous grenades, laden murderers, peevish caltrops and rascal desperadoes, which the Prince of lies employs with all his skill and malice to maintain the walls and gates of his kingdom, when Truth would enter in with grace and peace to save forlorn sinners and distressed commonwealths. Witness the present deplorable estate of sundry states in Europe.

units.la: If this side be resolute, I turne me to the other.
units.tr: If this side is resolute, I turn to the other.

units.la: And Wee your Brethren, though we necessarily abide beyond Jordan, and remaine on the American Sea-coasts, will send up Armies of prayers to the Throne of Grace, that the God of power and goodnesse, would incourage your hearts, cover your heads, strengthen your arms, pardon your sinnes, save your soules, and blesse your families, in the day of Battell. Wee will also pray, that the same Lord of Hosts, would discover the Counsells, defeat the Enterprizes, deride the hopes, disdaine the insolencies, and wound the hairy scalpes of your obstinate Enemies, and yet pardon all that are unwillingly misled. Wee will likewise helpe you beleeve that God will be seene on the Mount, that it is all one with him, to save by many or few, and that he doth but humble and try you for the present, that he may doe you good at the latter end. All which hee bring to passe who is able to doe exceeding abundantly, above all we can aske or thinke, for his Truth and mercy sake in Jesus Christ.
units.tr: And we, your brethren, though we necessarily live beyond the Jordan and remain on the American seacoasts, will send up armies of prayers to the throne of grace, that the God of power and goodness would encourage your hearts, cover your heads, strengthen your arms, pardon your sins, save your souls, and bless your families in the day of battle. We will also pray that the same Lord of Hosts would expose the counsels, defeat the enterprises, mock the hopes, scorn the insolence, and wound the hairy scalps of your obstinate enemies, yet pardon all who are misled against their will. We will likewise help you to believe that God will be seen on the mount, that it is all one to him to save by many or by few, and that he humbles and tries you only for the present, so that he may do you good in the latter end. May he who is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think bring all this to pass, for his truth and mercy's sake in Jesus Christ.

units.la: Amen. Amen.
units.tr: Amen. Amen.

units.la: A Word of IRELAND: Not of the Nation universally, nor of any man in it, that hath so much as one haire of Christianity or Humanity growing on his head or beard, but onely of the truculent Cut-throats, and such as shall take up Armes in their Defence.
units.tr: A Word about IRELAND: Not about the nation universally, nor about any man in it who has so much as one hair of Christianity or humanity growing on his head or beard, but only about the savage cut-throats and those who shall take up arms in their defence.

units.la: These Irish anciently called Antropophagi, man-eaters: Have a Tradition among them, That when the Devill shewed our Saviour all the kingdomes of the Earth and their glory, that he would not shew him Ireland, but reserved it for himself: it is probably true, for he hath kept it ever since for his own peculiar; the old Fox, foresaw it would eclipse the glory of all the rest: he thought it wisdome to keep it for a Boggards for himselfe, and all his unclean spirits imployed in this Hemisphere, and the people, to doe his Son and Heire, I mean the Pope, that service for which Lewis the eleventh kept his Barber Oliver, which makes them so blood-thirsty. They are the very Offall of men, Dregges of Mankind, Reproach of Christendome, the Bots that crawle on the Beasts taile, I wonder Rome it self is not ashamed of them.
units.tr: These Irish were anciently called Antropophagi, man-eaters. They have a tradition among them that when the Devil showed our Saviour all the kingdoms of the earth and their glory, he would not show him Ireland but reserved it for himself. It is probably true, for he has kept it ever since as his own peculiar possession; the old fox foresaw that it would eclipse the glory of all the rest. He thought it wise to keep it as a bogland for himself and all his unclean spirits employed in this hemisphere, and the people to do that service for his Son and Heir, I mean the Pope, for which Lewis the eleventh kept his barber Oliver; this is what makes them so blood-thirsty. They are the very offal of men, the dregs of mankind, the reproach of Christendom, the bots that crawl on the beast's tail. I wonder that Rome itself is not ashamed of them.

units.la: I begge upon my hands and knees, that the Expedition against them may be undertaken while the hearts and hands of our Souldiery are hot, to whom I will be bold to say briefly: Happy is he that shall reward them as they have served us,and Curled be he that shall do that work of the Lord negligently, Cursed be he that holdeth back his Sword from blood; yea, Cursed be he that maketh not his Sword starke drunk with Irish blood, that doth not recompence them double for their hellish treachery to the English, that maketh them not heaps upon heaps, and their Country a dwelling place for Dragons, an Astonishment to Nations: Let not that eye look for pity, nor that hand to be spared, that pities or spares them, and let him be accursed, that curseth not them bitterly.
units.tr: I beg upon my hands and knees that the expedition against them may be undertaken while the hearts and hands of our soldiery are hot. To them I will be bold to say briefly: happy is he who shall reward them as they have served us; and cursed be he who does the work of the Lord negligently; cursed be he who holds back his sword from blood; yea, cursed be he who does not make his sword stark drunk with Irish blood, who does not repay them double for their hellish treachery to the English, who does not make them heaps upon heaps and their country a dwelling place for dragons, an astonishment to nations. Let that eye look for no pity, and that hand expect no sparing, that pities or spares them; and let him be accursed who does not curse them bitterly.

units.tr: In every matter a brave and bold man is the better, even if he is a stranger and has come from distant shores.

units.tr: Many words will be reborn that have already fallen, and those that now stand in honour will fall, if usage wills it. Horace.

units.la: I honour them with my heart, that can expresse more than ordinary matter in ordinary words: it is a pleasing eloquence, them more, that study wisely and soberly to inhance their native language; them most of all, that esteeme the late significant speech, the third great blessing of the Land; it being so enriched; that a man may speake many tongues in his mothers mouth; and an uplandish Rusticke, more in one word than himselfe and all the Parish understands. Affe-ected &ted termes are unaffecting things to solid hearers; yet I hold him prudent, that in these faftidious times, will helpe difedged appetites with convenient condiments, and bangled ears, with pretty quicke pluckes. I speake the rather becaufe, not long fince, I met with a book, the beft to mee I ever faw, but the Bible ; yet under favour, it was fomewhat underclad, efpecially by him who can both excogitate and expreffe what hee undertakes, as well as any man I know. The world is growne so fine in words and witt, That pens must now Sir Edward Nich'las it. He that much matter speaks, speakes ne'r a whitt. If's tongue doth not carreer't above his witt.
units.tr: I honour with all my heart those who can express more than ordinary matter in ordinary words. It is a pleasing eloquence; I honour more those who study wisely and soberly to enrich their native language, and most of all those who esteem the lately significant speech, the third great blessing of the land, it being so enriched that a man may speak many tongues in his mother's mouth, and an upland rustic may understand more in one word than himself and all the parish. Affected and ted terms are unaffecting things to solid hearers; yet I hold him prudent who, in these fastidious times, will help jaded appetites with convenient condiments, and jangled ears with pretty quick plucks. I speak the rather because, not long since, I met with a book, the best I ever saw to me, except the Bible; yet, with respect, it was somewhat underdressed, especially by one who can both conceive and express what he undertakes as well as any man I know. The world has grown so fine in words and wit that pens must now, Sir Edward Nicholas, polish it. He who speaks much matter speaks never a whit. If his tongue does not career above his wit.

units.la: --Deductum dicere Carmen, is highly commended by Macrobius.
units.tr: --To sing a finely drawn-out song is highly commended by Macrobius.

units.la: Virgil himselfe said, Agrestem tenui meditabor arundine musam. Poetry's a gift wherein but few excell; He doth very ill, that doth not passing well. But he doth passing well, that doth his best, And he doth best, that passeth all the rest.
units.tr: Virgil himself said, I shall meditate the rustic Muse on a slender reed. Poetry is a gift in which few excel. He does very ill who does not do passing well. But he does passing well who does his best, and he does best who surpasses all the rest.

units.la: Quisquis inops peccat, minor est reus. Petron.
